extracted.intended_audience: employers, legal counsel, labor organizations, HR professionals, and other stakeholders affected by non-compete clauses and the FTC's rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and scope of the FTC's final rule defining 'non-compete clause' (§ 910.1) including examples, exclusions, and related definitions (garden leave, NDAs, TRAPs, international scope, workplace policies, etc.). Intended to guide application and compliance with the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compete clause — three-prong definition
rubrics_metrics.description: § 910.1 defines “non-compete clause” as a term or condition of employment that either “prohibits” a worker from, “penalizes” a worker for, or “functions to prevent” a worker from (A) seeking or accepting work in the United States with a different person where such work would begin after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition; or (B) operating a business in the United States after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three prongs — prohibits, penalizes, functions to prevent — are intended to be consistent with existing legal tests and capture express prohibitions, financial penalties or forfeitures tied to post-employment work, and overly broad or onerous terms that have the same functional effect as a prohibition. Application of the functional prong is fact-specific and may require case-by-case adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibits prong (express prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies to terms and conditions that expressly prohibit a worker from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business after their employment ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: contractual term forbidding a worker from working for another sandwich shop within three miles for two years; executive prohibited from working for any competing business anywhere in the world for one year. The Commission notes most existing agreements fall into this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalizes prong (financial penalties or forfeitures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies to terms that require a worker to pay a penalty or suffer financial consequences for seeking or accepting other work or starting a business after employment ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: liquidated damages provision (e.g., $50,000), forfeiture-for-competition clauses that extinguish promised compensation or benefits, severance arrangements paid only if the worker refrains from competing. Payments to prospective competitors to stay out of the market may also raise antitrust issues even if not technically non-competes under the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions to prevent prong (functional/ de facto non-competes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Captures terms that, while not expressly prohibiting or penalizing post-employment work, are so broad or onerous in scope that they functionally prevent a worker from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business after employment ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prong does not categorically prohibit other restrictive agreements (e.g., NDAs, TRAPs, non-solicitation) but ensures those that have the same practical effect as non-competes are covered. Determination is fact- and context-specific; courts already sometimes analyze overly broad covenants under non-compete tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) — when they are not vs. are non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: A garden-variety NDA that limits disclosure of certain confidential information generally is not a non-compete where its prohibitions do not apply to (1) information arising from a worker's general training/skill/experience or (2) information readily ascertainable by other employers or the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, NDAs that bar disclosure of any information 'usable in' or 'relating to' the industry, or bar disclosure of any knowledge obtained during employment (including public information), may be so broadly written that they functionally prevent a worker from working in the same field and thus qualify as non-competes under § 910.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-solicitation, no-hire, and no-business agreements — functional test
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally not non-compete clauses because they restrict who a worker may contact rather than where a worker can work, but they can meet § 910.1's definition if they function to prevent a worker from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business after employment ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether such agreements are non-competes is a fact-specific inquiry; they remain subject to section 5's prohibition on unfair methods of competition irrespective of whether covered by the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRAPs (training-related or repayment provisions) — potential functional non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: TRAPs that impose significant repayment obligations or penalties tied to leaving employment can function to prevent a worker from leaving and therefore may be non-competes under § 910.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: entry-level IT staffing TRAP requiring payment of >$20,000; nurse TRAPs requiring repayment of earnings plus future profits and other costs if leaving. The Commission declined to categorically prohibit or exempt TRAPs at this time, noting the evidentiary record primarily concerns non-competes and may not reveal legitimate uses of some TRAPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden leave — when covered vs. not covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a 'garden leave' arrangement is a non-compete depends on its form: arrangements where the worker remains employed and receives the same total annual compensation and benefits on a pro rata basis are not post-employment restrictions and thus not non-competes under the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, severance or post-employment payments conditioned on refraining from competing (e.g., severance paid only if worker does not work for competitor) would be penalizing and thus non-competes. The Commission declines to adopt a universal durational limit or rule for garden leave and will not opine on every factual scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severance, forfeiture, bonus-repayment, and accrued-benefit clauses — when not non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Clauses requiring repayment of a bonus or loss of accrued benefits are not non-competes under § 910.1 where they do not penalize or function to prevent a worker from seeking or accepting work or operating a business after employment ends and where repayment does not exceed the value of the bonus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: repayment of a bonus if a worker leaves before a certain time is not a non-compete if amount is no more than the bonus and the term is not tied to post-employment employment or business-starting restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: International scope — U.S.-limited application
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule expressly limits the definition of non-compete clause to terms that prevent workers from seeking or accepting work in the United States or operating a business in the United States; it does not apply to non-competes that restrict only work outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission chose a bright-line rule limited to U.S. work rather than a balancing test for extraterritorial restrictions. The final rule may still apply to overseas employers if the non-compete purports to restrict work or starting a business in the U.S. and a reviewing court applies U.S. law. The Commission declined to add a choice-of-law provision to prevent perceived evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace policies, handbooks, and oral representations included
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition uses the phrase 'a term or condition of employment' (not 'contractual term') and clarifies that it includes 'a contractual term or workplace policy, whether written or oral.' Clauses that purport to bind a worker are covered whether written or oral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission found that restrictions in handbooks or policies can have the same tendency to restrict mobility as formal contracts. § 910.2(a)(1) and (2) make it an unfair method of competition to make representations that a worker is subject to a non-compete, though such representations are not prohibited where there is a good-faith basis to believe the rule is inapplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent-employment restraints and fixed-duration contracts excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not extend to restraints on concurrent employment (e.g., moonlighting prohibitions) and clarifies fixed-duration employment contracts (agreements to remain employed for a fixed term) are not non-compete clauses because they do not restrain post-employment conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission declined to cover concurrent-employment restraints given the evidentiary record principally relates to post-employment restraints, and made a technical edit clarifying the rule targets restrictions tied to post-employment work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope across employer/worker arrangements (staffing agencies, third-party hiring)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule applies to a non-compete 'after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition,' clarifying coverage extends to situations where workers are hired by one party but work for another (e.g., staffing agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This revision addresses concerns about evasion through third-party hiring and ensures such clauses are unambiguously covered when the employment that includes the restrictive term concludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'person' in regulatory text
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule defines 'person' as 'any natural person, partnership, corporation, association, or other legal entity within the Commission's jurisdiction, including any person acting under color or authority of State law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adopts the cross-referenced statutory language plus 'within the Commission's jurisdiction' to clarify which entities are subject to the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of senior executives (existing non-competes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission adopts a different approach for 'senior executives' with respect to existing non-competes entered into before the final rule's effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chunk introduces this topic but details are in the subsequent text (not in this chunk). The rule signals differentiated treatment for senior executives versus other workers for pre-existing covenants.
